narrative: A Palestinian Syrian in his late twenties, born in the Yarmouk neighborhood of Damascus, described himself as a refugee twice over: his family first became refugees in 1948, fleeing Palestine in the Nakba and settling in Yarmouk. He worked as a typist in his uncle's publishing house, then as an editor at a Palestinian magazine, but could not afford university. When the Syrian revolution began, Yarmouk residents sheltered more than 200,000 displaced Syrians in their homes, schools and hospitals - refugees taking in refugees. In early 2012 he and his brothers sent their parents and little sisters to relatives in Lebanon; it was the last time he saw them, as Lebanon then closed its border to Palestinians. On 17 December 2012 Yarmouk was shelled and became a front line. For six months he lived under partial siege, crossing regime and opposition checkpoints every day under the eyes of snipers to find food, risking a gun rather than starving. In June 2013 he left the camp for the Damascus neighborhood of Qudsia, renting a flat with his girlfriend; they both worked at the same magazine for $175 a month against $200 rent. About a year later a friend offered a way out through a smuggler, even though as a Palestinian he could not enter Lebanon or Jordan and had no papers. His girlfriend, a Christian who would be in grave danger if discovered by ISIS, agonized for two months before agreeing: 'If you want to go, I will be with you.' On 1 September 2014 they left at 7 a.m., driving more than 13 hours with seven friends and some 50 others, the smuggler at the wheel, passing 47 regime checkpoints and paying over $50 per person in bribes. They drove through the destruction of Homs and Hama, then into ISIS territory, where at a checkpoint a boy soldier whose gun was taller than him checked the men's identity cards while the women moved to the back of the bus. They reached Manbij at 8 p.m. and were handed to a second smuggler, who drove them to the Turkish border and told them to walk one mile through the darkness with no light and no phone, because the Turkish police were watching. They walked for an hour; every step, he felt, was losing one of his memories of the country. Then someone whispered, 'It's Turkey.' Later he received a three-year residence permit in Germany and settled in a small town in the east.
